utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Good morning, Mr. Brdjanin. As usual, I address myself to you first. Can you hear me in a language you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, General Talic. I put the same question to you. THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, everybody. We start with the appearances. Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Andrew Cayley and Denise Gustin, case manager, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Defence for Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. With me are Tania Radosavljevic, Milka Maglov and Milos Peric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic, lawyer from the Paris Bar. I'm replacing Mr. de Roux and Mr. Pitron, and I'm assisted by Fabien Masson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we can continue from where we left yesterday, but before, I would like to be updated on the four motions by Mr. Ackerman. I was assured yesterday, towards the end of the hearing, that the few final documents were being made available, so I suppose they should be of some use.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I received this morning in my box downstairs some additional material, I believe, on Witness 99. With regard to the other, I guess it's three -- or two or three motions, I think there are still some outstanding matters there and there may be some outstanding on 99. I'm not positive about that. No. I'm told they are all in with 99, so we'll certainly be prepared to go forward with that next witness without any difficulty at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I recall Mr. Inayat, can I just go back to the Rule 92 issue and offer the Prosecution's apologies to Your Honour? As I've told the Defence, we were contacted yesterday and we discovered that in our hurry we had made rather a mess of the papers we had given to Your Honour. And we've provided a copy of the letter that when we returned the papers we gave to Your Honours on the subject. Can I just explain so that everybody understands? The witnesses, when they made the declarations, were dealing with the statement which had been translated into the Bosnian language, plus any attachments. Obviously, they couldn't read the English so it had to be in their own language. But what we provided to Your Honour now is just English versions, I hope. Obviously, if Your Honours require to see the actual Bosnian ones, we can provide them but you can't read them so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First of all, we can't read them. Secondly, I don't see why we should bother with that unless there is a very special reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which we don't have anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will recall Mr. Inayat straight away. I'm sorry, one further matter. We discussed, after the Court had risen yesterday, this question of the numbering of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, at the moment, the exhibits that I'm going through are those which the Defence take objection to their admission, and no doubt they are going to explain to Your Honour the grounds for it when we've finished. And so we considered the matter with the Deputy Registrar and thought it would probably be better if the actual numbering took place after Your Honours have admitted such -- all or such part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we will refer to them for the transcript by their disclosure number and describe what the document is so that one can see on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, I discussed this a little bit this morning with Madam Registrar, and more or less we are in agreement that that should be the approach unless Mr. Ackerman comes up with some novel idea which is better than yours and mine. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, here is -- maybe I'm not -- I'm missing something but I don't think so. Some appeals lawyer who has never heard of this case five years from now is -- or three years from now or whenever it is, is working on the appeal in this case. And he's able to find in the transcript that Exhibit P84 was admitted. And so he looks for the transcript portion where it was offered and whether there were any arguments against it, whether there was a proper objection made to it or not, and he can't find it because it's not P84 at that point. It's some other number. And he has no way to know what that number is. Unless we create some kind of an elaborate scheme of double numbering or something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can't possibly go into that much detail. My suggestion is that at the moment there is a document which is being contested. That document will be numbered. In other words, while we will be dealing with this mass of documents, there may be an incident at some point in time relating to a particular -- one particular document from that mass. If the documents would not have already been numbered until then, waiting for them to be renumbered -- to be numbered later on, then we will have to number it then. Because obviously what Mr. Ackerman is saying is that there must be some point of reference when the question -- okay. I've made the same mistake now. I apologise to the interpreters. Let me hear what you have to say. I mean, we have to find a way which will make it easy for everyone and also keeping in mind that later on, after this trial is over, whoever will be dealing with the appeal - if there is an appeal, as Mr. Ackerman has suggested already that there will be - will obviously have to deal with a humongous number of documents. And the references must be clear and unequivocal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just continue for just a second before Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know that what the registry wants is for a different number to be attached to documents which are admitted from those which are not admitted. I think that's the registry's position. What I'm saying to you is that is not -- that doesn't make sense, in terms of the record. There is absolutely nothing wrong with there being a document called P84, and either it is admitted or it's not admitted but it remains P84 from the moment we begin talking about it until the moment we're finished talking about it. So you can always do a search of the record and find every instance where P84 was discussed. You can do an electronic search and find that, and that solves every problem there is. It's just a matter of giving it one number the first time we talk about it and keeping that number absolutely all the time. And if it's admitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that is necessary, important, yes. And that's how it's going to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then I have no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the only problem arises if there is a lack of proper identification of that particular document, in other words, if it is referred to by the Prosecution by a particular number and then it is referred to by the Defence in a different number. So that's the only problem that can arise. But I don't envisage it happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the difficulty is --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. Because you all speak English, can you please slow down so that the French interpreter and B/C/S interpreter can catch up with you all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm perfectly aware that Ms. Fauveau speaks excellent English, but I appreciate the problem with the B/C/S. Your Honour, the difficulty is this: If they're all numbered with a "P," as we go -- as each document is mentioned, then it is not clear whether it has been admitted or has not been admitted when you look at the transcript. That's the real problem. In addition, at the moment I'm not -- I'm following the order of the documents to which objection is taken. If they are numbered as I refer to them, then the whole sequence will go out of order, and it will be just as difficult. My suggestion is - and I'm not clear what the difficulty is - that for the purposes of the transcript, I will refer to them by their disclosure number plus a description of what the document is. If Your Honour decides to admit into evidence the whole bundle of documents that Dr. Donia is going to refer to, obviously, you will certainly be admitting some into evidence because no objection is taken. Then they will be numbered. At the end of the day, it will not be difficult to sort out the appropriate court number because there will be a full index which will show that document, whatever it is now, P1, P2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour, that simply does not work. To try to rely on some kind of a subsequently prepared index, we tried that. The index of documents in the Delalic case was absolutely completely out of whack. What the index set of documents was had nothing to do with what the document was. Part of that had to do with changing court deputies several times during the trial. And I think there was some confusion with that. But whatever it was, it didn't work, and it was mess at the end of the case. There is nothing wrong, I submit to you, to take these documents that are in these books and take the first document in the book and call it P3 and subsequently number every number P4, P5, P6, P7. So if she's talking about a document this morning that I'm objecting to, that document might be P9. And at the end of this whole process, you will decide that whatever number of these are admitted and whatever number of them are not, and the record will be clear that P4 was admitted, that at page 175 it was objected to, at page 217 it was admitted. But if you start creating a system where what you have to do to find all of those references to that is search three or four different numbers, like 2.273, the Prosecutor's number, or P8, the registry's number, or BD something or other which would be the line number, it just becomes unworkable. And we have to think about what the transcript is going to show, not what we see here in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I still think that what Ms. Korner suggested can work. There shouldn't be any difficulty. Because if this bundle here which constitutes the totality of the documents on which Dr. Donia will be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exhibit number P3 or whatever, then we can easily, easily provide that the integrity of this bundle remains unaffected. Then I don't see any difficulties because each document has got, I suppose, what is the disclosure number. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Each document has written across the top a disclosure number, except for the extra ones that were handed at the last moment. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Those, we can number. Those, we can number, and there should be no possibility for confusion because it would be document D6104 in bundle Exhibit P3.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I raised this here, and I'm going to have to back down on this. I bow to the greater experience of Mr. Cayley and Mr. Ackerman who have dealt with these trials before. They say it does become exceedingly difficult. So I'm afraid we're going to have to find some method of identifying the ones that Your Honours do not admit separately. But for the moment, it does seem -- as I go through each document, we should give it a number as I go through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So I'm sorry, it's my fault. But Mr. Cayley and Mr. Ackerman agree on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Would that create havoc with the registry?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Not really, Your Honour. And I just feel sorry that this kind of management of documents creates such a problem here. Before the trial start, we actually advise both parties to attend this trial management meeting which was providing the approaches how to manage all these documents. But at that time, it seems like all this Defence counsel, they don't want to attend this meeting, so that we can't reach this kind of agreement before the trial starts. But from the registry point of view, we normally separate two type of binders. One is for the admitted evidence, that is, exhibit. The other binders consist of all these non-admitted documents. So in the -- at the end of the trial, we can always find where is where. And plus the appeal number always is the official numbers for all these exhibits. So there's no difficulties whatsoever to find where this exhibits is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can work it like that, then. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was wholly unaware of anything called a trial management meeting. But I'm told by Ms. Gustin there was such a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Neither was I.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But nobody attended, apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's no problem. I mean, let's not look at what happened in the past months, and look forward -- don't look behind when the journey lies ahead, they say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree. I just have to say that the meeting that was suggested to me was characterised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forget it, Mr. Ackerman. Don't take it as a criticism. I'm just suggesting not to look behind when your journey lies ahead. More or less, we have now agreed on the system that should be followed and we will follow that system. So please call witness Mazhar Inayat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, when he comes in, I think I'll have to go back over the documents that we've discussed and just give them a number as we go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. No problem. If you need some time for that, you will have ample time for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So can I give some numbers to yesterday's documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first one is 00403850, and that should be --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, no. That isn't going to work. If we are going to number them - I'm sorry - then we ought to go through the bundle numbering them sequentially, even the ones which aren't disputed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I just want to finish up yesterday's business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Inayat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will now be asked to make the same solemn declaration you made yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, and Ms. Korner from the Prosecution will be resuming her examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, just to let you know we are going to just go back to the beginning of the bundle of documents. You needn't reply because I'm just going to get them numbered on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first document in the bundle, which is a -- in the Serbian language only, which was numbered 00403770, will become P3. Your Honour, it's -- I understand that each document, whether it's in English or in the Serbian language, has to have a slightly separate number so Your Honour can identify which one one is looking at, so that if we can cause the English P3, for example, A, and the B/C/S, P3B. There is only a B/C/S one here, so that would be P3B. The second document in the bundle, which has the disclosure number 1.118, will become P4 in English -- P4A in English and P4B in B/C/S. The third document, with the disclosure number 1.119, will become P5, A and B. The next document, with the disclosure number 7.221, P6, A and B. The next document is only in the Serbian language. It has the number 00403782, becomes P7B. Then the next document is 7.221, which will become Exhibit 8, A and B. The next document -- I'm sorry, I better distinguish. They bear the same disclosure number. 7, A and B, was the decision on the municipality of Laktasi, joining the Bosanska Krajina community, yes, 7. And then document 8, A and B, is the decision on the conclusion of the agreement by Bosanska Gradiska. The next document, Your Honour, now this is the subject of objection, but I understand the objection was purely the lack of translation, from Mr. Ackerman, so that will be 9, P9B, and it's got a number 00403700. Your Honour, the next one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because there is something wrong here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go back. Yes, Ms. Korner, pleases, let's go back to document behind tab 4, which has number 00403782.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That, according to the sequence in my bundle ought to be document P7B. Are you suggesting another number?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I've lost track.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Same here. So -- but we need to be in consonance and the reference numbers must be the same. Otherwise we'll get confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Might it make sense, Your Honour, for us to take a 15 or 20 minute break and let us work all these numbers out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I was going to suggest to Ms. Korner to take them ten at a time for the time being and see if there are any problems with those ten, and then proceed with the next ten, and we will do it like that and make sure we know which documents we are talking about, okay? So this -- I'm correct here, this should be document P7B.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Behind tab 5 is a document which I have in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this is the decision on the municipality of Laktasi joining the Bosanska Krajina municipalities. It is 00403783 and that disclosure number 7.221, and that according to me, or according to the sequence that I have here, should be P8A, correct? With the B/C/S version P8B, correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So now, the next document that I have, between tabs 6 and 7, is the decision on the conclusion of the agreement to join -- the Bosanska Gradiska municipality decision to join the Bosanska Krajina, and this is 0040 -- I suppose it's 3925 or 39 -- I don't know, I can't see the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think it matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This would be P9A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the B/C/S version, which follows, would be P9B, correct? And I think you can take it up from here now and continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour this was -- the next document only in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which Mr. Ackerman complained about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. But I think it's only because of lack of translation and we will get it translated. So that's P10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P10B.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's stop here for the moment. Are you happy with this classification for reference purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm just absolutely struck with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Delighted? Exhilarated?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next document with the disclosure number 1.53, is objected to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How are we going to mark - I ask for guidance from anybody - a document that at the moment Your Honour hasn't ruled on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. What is your suggestion, Madam Registrar, in this regard?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would like to suggest remain as it is, 1.53, OTP document, if it has not been admitted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But then if it's not admitted, it's going to be removed from this file and it goes into a separate file.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Another binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Another binder, and will you give it then another separate number or will it always remain as it is document OTP 1.53?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1.53, unless you want to give it another mark for identification number, MFI and MFI1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MFI.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would help because if -- at the end of the day, we are going to ask Your Honour for a ruling. If it stays out of the sequence until the ruling, then the numbering will be completely out of sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is what I want to avoid.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would suggest that we call it P11, I think we've got to, slash MMI or whatever the thing is, MFI? Marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is the difficulty if it becomes P11? Then ultimately, if this Chamber decides to -- not to admit it, and it goes in the other binder, it remains P11 over there as well but in the index that you will have, you will have an annotation, "P11 moved to unadmitted documents"? And the index in that case would start with P11. I think we can work like that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I take your point. I'm just trying to differentiate between this exhibit and that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. That was a suggestion that was made to me in the first place before I started this trial, but I thought it would confuse matters rather than simplify them. The reason is very simple, that now counsel will be referring to that document. How are they going to refer to it? Because it has the potentiality of being admitted or of not being admitted and it can't have two references. Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're absolutely right. We have a spreadsheet here that has a column in it. It has the number of the exhibit and whether or not it was admitted. It's simple. You just say admitted, yes or no. But you maintain that same number sequence regardless of whether it's admitted or not. Otherwise the record is a mess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's the way we should follow. That's the way I am used to, but I don't want to create new systems here, but I think it makes sense to follow that pattern, that system. Can you live with that, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm quite happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. This will be P11, P11A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because there is also a version of it in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is. And Your Honour, I remind -- yes, that this one is subject to a challenge. Your Honour, that was the last document we dealt with yesterday in evidence. The next document, with the disclosure number 1.59, Your Honour, is also subject to challenge. It will become P11A --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P12A and B.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, could you tell us where the Office of the Prosecutor acquired that document?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please once again have the ERN number?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The original is 00403854.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was also handed to one of our investigators, Mr. Grant MacIntosh, on 25th of April, 1996, by Mr. Boro Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, can I ask you a simple question. Will you be producing Mr. Grant MacIntosh later on as a witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've never actually heard of Mr. Grant MacIntosh until now -- or rather, from Mr. Inayat. But I gather he's a investigator who left the OTP some -- well, perhaps Mr. Inayat can explain who or what Mr. MacIntosh was.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Grant MacIntosh was an investigator from the United States of America, and he worked with Team 1, that is, the team that I'm working on now, and probably left sometime at the end of -- in the summer of 1997. So he's not working in the Tribunal any more for the last three or four years now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Your Honour felt it necessary, no doubt we could make inquiries and bring him back here to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But as I understand it, Mr. Inayat, the records that were kept show that he received this document on this date. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The records that I have checked clearly indicate that Mr. MacIntosh took possession of this document on 25th of April, 1996 in Banja Luka personally from Mr. Boro Blagojevic. That's what the records state very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In one sense, Your Honour, it might be quicker to witness summons, if Your Honour feels this is necessary, Mr. Blagojevic and bring him here from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Korner, as you know, I come from a jurisdiction where we interfere very little with the way the Prosecution conducts its own case and the way the Defence conducts its defence. So it's up to you. But certain decisions will have to be taken by you with no interference from this Chamber, anyway. What I would also like to know is whether these records that you are referring to and which you have consulted are easily available to us in case we require them or in case the Defence need to verify them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

What happens is whenever we receive any evidence, the investigator who receives it in his possession is supposed to fill out information index form, or also called the IF. And there's a very exhaustive IF database. And that is the database that I have referred to to find out the sources for all these documents. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I wasn't commenting on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we're not concerned with that matter or problem for the time being. What we are concerned at the time being with is the source as it is being confirmed and explained by witness and any questions of -- preliminary questions as to admissibility if these arise, if and when.

utterances.text: I totally agree with that. All I was suggesting is that the Chamber might someday want to know this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I told you already, Mr. Ackerman, and I told Ms. Korner that we want to interfere very little. I mean, the onus of the burden of proof which rests with the Prosecution is well known to the Prosecution, and your position is also one which does not need any elucidation from this Chamber. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC

utterances.text: Well, I haven't on my marking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I really must ask that both Defence counsel now adopt the same system, which is a simpler one, not what we do not object to but what we do. Because I think what's happened is because Mr. Ackerman was doing it different, we have in fact made some confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We also challenge this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of us is French and one of us is American, and we're supposed to do it different, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I definitely will not get Ms. Korner to answer that question. So we take it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will take it, Ms. Korner, that this is being objected to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, that's disclosure number 2.274.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document given again by Mr. Boro Blagojevic on 26th of April, 1996. Mr. Grant MacIntosh received it in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The next document --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- P43. Although I have no note that it's objected to, I imagine that it is, because it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't imagine so. I would be very surprised, because the document that I have, if we are talking about the same document, that is, the 14th July 1992 document bears the signature of Mr. Kupresanin and also the stamp of the country that -- in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it seems to be the Assembly of the Autonomous --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry. I was looking -- you're right. It does. So that's P43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do I take it that there is no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I don't think I advised Ms. Korner that I objected to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I have no objection to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we do not object to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P44 is the next document. 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, this is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's probably not P40. Let's call it P43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 44, it would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 44. 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, this bears the same signature and stamp. So I take the position is the same as before. No objection to this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. No foundation for objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just so -- because in order to deal with some of the issues Your Honour raised yesterday in the judgement to add to the weight --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, where did this document, disclosure number 2.277, come from?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was also given by Mr. Boro Blagojevic to Mr. MacIntosh on 25th of April, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The next document, P45, no objection. That's the 22nd of April, 1992 public announcement. The next document, P46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, 46. Again, there should be no objection here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour is right. Just for the purposes of the record, 2.27 is the disclosure number. The next document, dated the 13th of May, again no objection, P47. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I gave Ms. Korner a list of documents that we'd suggest are the signature of Ms. Brdjanin. If this was in that list, then we do not contest it on that basis. If it wasn't in that list, then we do. The list is complete, as far as I know. And if there's any change, I will advise her, but I can't do it standing on my feet right here now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Your Honour, that was P47. The next document, P48, is objected to, disclosure number 2.272.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that's withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This bears the signature of Kupresanin, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Foundation is waived, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The next document, which is a fax message, is not objected to. That is P49. A fax message, I should say, dated the 7th of May, 1992. P50, minutes. Now, according to my note, this is objected to. It's the 12th of May session, Banja Luka, disclosure number 2.257.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I would like to address this question to the Defence teams. There seems to be -- it seems to me that this document in its B/C/S version on page 5 bears the stamp of the Republika Srpska and also the signature of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Krajisnik. Do you maintain your objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right now, Your Honours, I must maintain it, because I simply can't figure out what the relationship is between the first five pages and the balance of the document. That may be clear to everyone in the courtroom but me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Mr. Ackerman looks at page 4 of the English translation, he will see there "President of the Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik," signed, stamped.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just can't make heads or tails of what happens after page 5, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It probably is authentic, but I can't say so right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I heard the Exhibit number being stated as 2.257.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's I think 2.21.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 2.21. Sorry, my fault.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2.21, yes. This document was given to us by the secretary of the RS assembly, Mr. Rajko Stanisic, on 6th of February, 1998 in Pale. And this was received by staff of the Officer of the Prosecutor personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P51 is a -- a military document with the number 4.972 disclosure. And that's objected to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, where did we get that?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the exhibit number once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The disclosure number is 4.972.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this is -- before you reply, Mr. Inayat. And Mr. Ackerman and Ms. Fauveau, I refer you to the first and last pages of the B/C/S version of this document. On the first page there on top right, there seems to be a stamp of the 1st Partisan Brigade with a handwritten insert, including the date. On the last page, there is also what is purported to be the signature of Momcilo Dmitrovic. Do you maintain or sustain the objection, or would you like to withdraw it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I didn't object.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's Ms. Fauveau for General Talic who objected.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I maintain my objection, Your Honours, because it seems that this stamp on the first page does not correspond to the person who signed the document, and the persons in the document do not correspond to the brigade. So I might withdraw my objection if I know the source of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So -- Mr. Inayat.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Disclosure number 4.972, this particular document was given to us by the BiH embassy through their liaison officer on the 31st of October, 1996, and the person who received it in the Office of the Prosecutor is Mr. Johan Du Toit, who is still currently working in the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact, he's a lawyer working for the Prosecutor, Your Honour. Then the final document, Your Honour, of the minutes or an excerpt from the transcript of the 50th session of the Assembly of the Republika Srpska, they are objected to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, I think you can confirm that this document was personally handed to Mr. O'Donnell. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please tell me the exhibit number of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was referred to in the statement made by Mr. O'Donnell. It's 00845781. Disclosure number, I'm sorry, 2.424.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you look at the original list, Mr. Inayat, you'll see it's referred to with the ERN numbers. It's the last -- if you look at the handwritten note, it's the last document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document that was given to Mr. O'Donnell. And I believe this was personally given by Mr. Rajko Stanisic, the secretary of the RS assembly. And Mr. O'Donnell received this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In addition, Mr. O'Donnell would have testified to the fact that a statement was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it's appropriate for Ms. Korner to tell you what he would have testified to. That makes her a witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is the objection maintained?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, he is right. Let's go ahead. Are you finished with the witness for the moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm asking if the objection is maintained. I don't want to spend any time proving these things more strictly than I have to, but I will. Is the objection to this -- to the admissibility of this document maintained?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, among other things, I have what might be a ten-page English version and what might be a 200-page B/S/C version. It's impossible to correlate the two. And so, you know, who knows what's not -- it just takes time to work it out. But in any event, there's no signatures or anything like that on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that's the position. And we'll take it as the objection being maintained. Yes, that's the last document. What we have there is a translation into English of Mr. Kupresanin's speech, and the rest obviously contains much more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is the P52, the full -- I'm sorry, a partial English translation of the 50th session of the Assembly of the Republika Srpska, but the full transcript is there in the original. Your Honour, those are the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you would have objected had the Prosecution not disclosed the full transcript of the meeting in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, that would have been worse than what we have now, probably. May I make a request at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat has, throughout his testimony, referred to and used as a source of information documents - I can't remember what he called them, they are exhibit indexes or something like that - documents that were prepared by the person to whom the document was handed, as a contemporaneous record of that process, and, for example, this MacIntosh or McGregor, or whatever his name is, from the United States who received all these documents from Blagojevic made records at the time that the witness has been referring to. For the purposes of cross-examination, I would ask that copies of those records that the witness has been referring to be provided to me so I can use them during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have an objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time. I don't think that there is any problem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have to break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- but may I take the opportunity at the break to consult and if necessary to make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because that concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There will now be a break of 25 minutes. We will resume at 5 past or 10 past 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So while we wait for Mr. Inayat, the decision on the Rule 92 bis motion will be handed later on in the day, early in the afternoon, I would suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Could I just mention that Mr. Inayat extracted the forms to which he's been referring, or a selection, and we've given them to Mr. Ackerman. They are not copied. They are internal forms and Mr. Ackerman has agreed to hand them back to us at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you will be continuing your evidence on the same solemn declaration that you entered first thing this morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've actually been given four forms. Does this cover all of the documents, these four forms?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a selection. We didn't realise that you wanted every single one of them. To extract the whole lot would have taken considerably more than the half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can I ask the basis upon which this selection was made, so I'll know what I'm dealing with here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Inayat made the selection. Perhaps he can just explain the basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine so, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, what I did was, when I was asked to bring these forms down -- first of all, I would have preferred to bring examples for all these documents. However, the computer was -- the network is very slow currently at this point. So what I did was I selected four documents at random, four ERN numbers at random, to give Mr. Ackerman some idea, and all those four forms are for documents that we spoke this morning about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you are prepared, are you not, to relate a form that I have to a particular document?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you give me the exhibit number and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can't go anywhere near that, but maybe you can. We'll get there eventually but I don't want to start that so we will do some other things first. Good morning, Mr. Inayat.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm John Ackerman. I'm counsel for Mr. Brdjanin in this case. And I have, I think, not very many questions for you. I want to take you back to your testimony yesterday where you were talking about the various searches and seizures that you did in connection with this case or in connection with maybe more than this case. The first one you talked about was a visit that you made to Prijedor, I believe, on 12 December, 1997?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of the things that I'm curious about is, when you would go, for instance, to the municipal building in Prijedor, what you were looking for, at least partially, were records from that municipality that were the kind of records that municipality would have kept in the regular course of its business?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you, in fact, found such records?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Every time you went to a municipality with a search warrant, whether it was in Prijedor or Banja Luka or any of the other places you might have gone, you would find those kinds of records?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the -- as far as the searches of municipal buildings in Prijedor and Banja Luka are concerned, we were able to seize more documents in Prijedor than in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And my question is: Were you able on, say, that first day in Prijedor, when you seized 53.000 pages of documents, were you able to copy all those and leave copies with the Prijedor municipality for their official records?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't do that. It was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you just took the records of that municipality and took them off to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. That is what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Does the Prijedor municipality -- it's just now trying to function without those records?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have not returned them any copies, so I guess so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I take it, then, if some historian were trying to conduct historical research regarding the events that happened in that area during the year 1992, they would have a very difficult time because none of those documents would be available to them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think the witness ought to be put in a position to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, he's not in a position to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you know -- as far as you know, the documents, the sole repository of those documents now is the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The evidence unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. How many -- do you have any idea how many boxes of documents that 53.000 pages that you took from Prijedor involved?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot give a precise number of boxes that we used, but there were definitely more than 20 boxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was it -- I mean, were they carried in a truck or a car, or do you know -- just to give the Tribunal some idea of what a mass this might have been.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say they were carried, you mean from Prijedor to Zagreb and then on to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were transported in a UN vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A truck?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: A big UN vehicle. Sort of a truck but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that -- oh, I take it that these searches were not announced in advance. You didn't call up these places in Prijedor and let them know you'd be there next week to do searches.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The moment you arrived at the scene was the first that they knew of a search being conducted.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local officials at those locations, they found out when we got there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You indicated that you had taken with you people from SFOR and the, I think, IPTP or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: IPTF.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: IPTF, for reasons that the area was not totally secure and there were concerns about safety and things of that nature with regard to your presence there and what it was you were doing.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's true, from the knowledge that you have, at least, from that incident, that the ethnic tensions that existed during the war had not dissipated completely by that time.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not so sure about the ethnic tensions at that time in 1997. All I tried to point out yesterday was that there was some reservations on our part as to how we will be received by the local officials and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- whether the searches will be allowed to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go -- and I think it will be sufficient just to refer generically to these information index forms. I take it this is a standard form that is used and has been used for some time by the investigative units of this -- of the Prosecutor's office when it gathers up evidence.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And just let me clarify, that before the introduction of the information index form, we had a similar procedure. And that form was called TIF. So from the very beginning, we have had this procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right. And just from looking at these forms, there is certain information that the one who prepares it, that -- I guess that's the person who is designated in the blank "created by." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you please let me have one copy, and then perhaps I can clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely. I assumed you had copies of all these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, do you want this document to be placed on the ELMO so that you can follow better?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm familiar with the form. I don't think we need -- but if Your Honours want to see it, maybe --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we should put it on the ELMO. I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Just one moment. Before that happens, it does occur to me that these are internal forms and not really intended for public dissemination, and therefore putting them on the ELMO automatically makes them public. I'm sorry that we didn't manage to get copies, but we can do copies very quickly so that Your Honour can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we can do actually -- we don't need to wait for copies. We can have a look at the document, and then we will know exactly what Mr. Ackerman is referring to and what Mr. Inayat will be responding to. Mr. Inayat, are you in a position to reply to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd request Mr. Ackerman to please repeat that question once more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's a space on the form where it says "created by," and then there are some letters that appear in there. I assume that identifies the person who created this particular index form.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That's his last name, and plus the initial of the first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And that would have been a person who was present at the time the document was seized, whether it was the thing you were doing there at the municipal building in Prijedor where you were making these records or -- or what. But the person would have been present when it was --

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not the case. Normally, a document would be created by an investigator who has received the documents. But if these are B/C/S documents and we don't understand the substance, then what we do is pass on the information to a special section where B/C/S language staff can create these documents for us. So most often you will find that the person who has created the document may not have actually been the person who has seized or received the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that person, the one I'm looking at, has a series of letters beginning with the letter "B," B-e -- and I -- and I don't think I should read it all. But begins with the letter "B," and that person then would receive information from the person who is designated as the receiver.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then transfer that information onto a form such as this.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So there must be some other form that is between the receiver and the information index form.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we have a large collection of documents that have to be IF-ed, that is, information indexed, what we do is we receive from the evidence unit a pre-IF form. That particular form has to be filled in by the person who has received these documents. What he will do is -- or she -- she will indicate where documents are received from, who received them, who submitted them, and this pre-IF form then will go along with the documents to the person who will create these IFs. So that person has the information. So we have the pre-IF forms also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If that person were to come to me, for instance, and I were to say, "I have these six documents for you," and I were to describe to him those documents and say, for instance, "These documents are drafts that were never circulated, but I thought you might like to have them," where is that recorded, or is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, are you aware of any such cases, to start with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally, Your Honours, I'm not aware of such a case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So are you in a position to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd rather not, because that may not be correct information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But my only question is: Is there, in the process by which you receive documents, is there a provision for recording in any way the representation that the person who turns over the document makes to the investigator at the time the document is turned over?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally have been present at three such searches where persons were giving us the documents. But perhaps I did point this out yesterday that the sheer amount of documents were so much that it was not possible for the person who was giving us the documents to get into these kind of details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I think maybe I -- I think the way I've asked the question has misled you, and I didn't mean to do that. Let me talk specifically about the situation where Grant MacIntosh was handed documents by Boro Blagojevic. Is there any provision in the way your office handles documents for Mr. MacIntosh to have recorded in any way what it was that Boro Blagojevic, the representations that he made about what these documents were?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me inform you that Mr. Boro Blagojevic indicated documents to Mr. Grant MacIntosh and other members of the staff. Members of the staff then went through those folders and identified the documents that they wanted. It wasn't that Mr. Boro Blagojevic was selecting those documents for us. The members of the Office of the Prosecutor selected those documents and when they came back, they submitted that evidence with the IF form.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So Mr. Blagojevic just gave investigators from your office access to a series of documents or a file of documents or files of documents?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And to your knowledge, there was never any communication between them and Mr. Blagojevic regarding what the documents actually were, what they represented, that he made no representations to them with regard to the documents, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Mr. Grant MacIntosh, if he's called, perhaps can answer that question. I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, another thing that I see on this form is -- if you go down into kind of the second section of the form where it has type, language, date, things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There are designations across there, "chain of custody, no." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the document was not seized under the procedure of chain of custody. That's what it means. Had it been seized under chain of custody procedures, then the answer would have been yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What are chain of custody procedures?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm told there is a senior investigator, Your Honours, in this Office of the Prosecutor who is currently a deputy investigation commander, who has been dealing with all chain of custody matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if -- I didn't think chain of custody was an issue, but if there is an issue on chain of custody, I will call the investigator who is qualified to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A question on what procedure was precisely followed in chain of custody is very pertinent, but I don't think the witness is in a position or should be asked that question. I don't think he is the person, the right person, to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not asking about any specific documents, Your Honour, but just what that particular blank means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But he is not the ideal person or the best evidence that you could have on the subject. I mean, you have the word of the Prosecution that should information be required on the procedure followed in chain of custody, that would be made -- that would be brought forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So as a team leader of an investigative team, you don't have information about what these things on here mean?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do. But I was only saying that I'm not qualified to give more exhaustive detailed information on chain of custody. I know that normally when we seize material during search and seizure operations, chain of custody procedures are followed, and that's what I was trying to explain yesterday also, that an evidence register form is created under the chain of custody procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you actually create these forms yourself at times, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I mean you specifically.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have created over a couple of hundred such forms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And one of the things that you have to complete when you do that is this question, chain of custody?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you must have some knowledge about what you're supposed to put there?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the knowledge - this is what I'm telling you - that if I have seized material in the field, and if these are original documents, like we did in 2000 October in Prijedor Police Station and some other places, we created those forms on the chain of custody and I put the answer here "yes," to show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Thank you. I assume the blank signed and certified referred to whether or not the document is signed and whether or not it's certified?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So if you acquire a document that has a signature on it, you would put "yes," it's signed; if you acquire a document that is certified as a true copy of a document that's in a record somewhere, you could put "yes" on certified?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. You've spoken -- I'm through now talking to you about these documents, Mr. Inayat. Thank you very much. You have spoken about an organisation called AID, and you've told us what AID stands for. Could you tell me again?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that AID stands for Agency for Investigation and Documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's an agency of what organisation?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formerly this agency was known as the State Security Service, the SDB, and in January of 1996, it was transformed and called Agency for Investigation and Documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Does it belong to an NGO or a government or --

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It belongs to -- it's a government agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of what government?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the BiH government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And their mission is to gather documents regarding events during the war? Is that what they are doing?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also to take statements from victims and witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So they are basically investigators of what happened during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And they work on behalf of the BiH government in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you talk about receiving documents from the MUP in Sarajevo, what you're talking about is the Bosnia-Herzegovina Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Fauveau, would you like to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have a few questions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I'm Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic and I represent General Talic. I would like us to go back to the documents seized in Banja Luka for a moment. You told us yesterday that these documents were seized simultaneously at different locations?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that you were in the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part of the day, yes, I was in the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you at any given moment at the Security Services Centre, in the radio building or in the presidential palace?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not visit any of those three locations that you've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, I will limit my questions to the town hall building. In the town hall, you said that you were together with representatives of SFOR and IPTF. Were there also any officials of the Republika Srpska present there?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise if I didn't mention that yesterday. For our own protection, the RS authorities also assigned RS police officers and they accompanied us throughout the search and seizure operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the seizure of documents, did you select documents or did you take all the documents? Did you make a selection?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did select documents. I mean, of course, there was a lot of material available to us, and of course, we couldn't have picked up everything. So we were making a random selection. So you are right. I mean, I confirm that selection was made to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us on the basis of which criteria you made that selection?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were, of course, interested basically in the 1991, 1992 period, documents pertaining to this specific period, and also early 1993. So as we were searching the material that was all made available to us, we had access to any place we wanted to go to, we were specifically looking for the material that was for 1991, 1992 and 1993. We were, of course, very keen to look for municipal assembly documents such as minutes, meetings, and memorandums, and similarly we were also interested in seeking out documents of the outgoing and the incoming correspondence between the municipal assembly and the municipal authorities, between other organs of the Banja Luka municipality. So -- but primarily we were focusing on the 1992, 1993 period, with the municipal assembly documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: During this seizure, did you use the official register of the municipality, the register of their documents?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I don't quite recall that such a register was made available to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When seizing these documents in the town hall building, can you confirm that all those documents were official documents of the municipality, or is it possible that there may have been private documents that happened to be among them?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer this question, I would just like to clarify myself on a previous question that you asked about the criteria. I need to point out that during our searches, we were also very keen to look for documents pertinent to the ARK assembly, the Autonomous Region of Krajina assembly, and the ARK Crisis Staff meetings, and we couldn't find really much on that. To your question, I believe I'll have to go and review the evidence register forms once again. I personally believe that most of the material that we seized was official, that consisted of official documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but my question was: Is it possible that among those documents there may have been one or two that were not official?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We seized over 145.000 pages of documents from the municipal building and the CSB, so I'm afraid I just can't say at this point of time that we may have seized a couple of documents that were private in nature and not official.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So it's possible, then, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I am not quite sure whether this is part of your competence, but I would like to know when this indication "ERN" was placed on the documents.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean specifically on the documents that were seized from the municipal building in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was, as I pointed out yesterday, seized on 27th of February, 1998. Then the documents were transported to the Tribunal. And it -- we started the scanning process very soon. And at that point the ERN numbers, the unique 16-digit numbers, were assigned to each and every page that was seized.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that this reference number was not placed on all the documents?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the documentation was transported to The Hague, the team immediately assigned log managers who took custody of this documentation. And I personally am not aware that any of the Banja Luka municipal documents escaped registration of ERN numbers. I personally am not aware of that, because I believe that the log managers did a very good job and controlled the documents thoroughly and in a very competent manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, it isn't something which is in Mr. Inayat's competence, but there are people available who can explain the stamping process, because it was handed over, as he says, to other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, Mr. Inayat is confirming that he is not aware of any such -- at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm asking this question because we have received so many CD-ROMs with 10.000 documents with no reference on them, and allegedly they come from the municipality building and the Banja Luka radio building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, that may be the case, but you can't expect Mr. Inayat to reply to your question if he is not -- if he doesn't have these documents in front of him. And in any case, one has to see first whether he is the person who could provide us with the correct explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say that if Ms. Fauveau wants an explanation of why they didn't have numbers, we can give it to her. But it's not something, as Your Honour says, this witness can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed with some other question, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: The documents given to you by AID or another physical or moral person, did those persons indicate the source from which they obtained those documents?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents that were given to us by the AID in Bihac, especially during November 1995 and April 1996, that's when -- the biggest collection has come from AID. The operatives who had seized the material gave us the information as to how these documents were received. The members of the Office of the Prosecutor even visited those premises from where those documents were seized. So they did give us this information as to when and how these documentation was seized.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this specific for AID of Bihac or also for other bodies, for example, the Ministry of the Interior or the Embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I should make it very clear that majority of the documents that have been given to us by AID offices outside Bihac, they deal with witness statements that the AID officials had taken of witnesses and victims. So it's quite clear, because the witnesses do mention at the beginning of their statement the time and date when they had been interviewed and the person who has interviewed them, so I must trust this that the majority of the documents given to us by AID are witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the Embassy of Bosnia and the Ministry of the Interior, what about those?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The biggest collection that has come from the Ministry of Interior, which we pointed out, the Sarajevo collection, those documents were identified. Almost, like, 23.000 pages of documents were identified by the Office of the Prosecutor -- staff from the Office of the Prosecutor. And we knew -- we had been told how this collection had come to the hands of the Ministry of Interior, so we are aware of where those documents have come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
